The document states that the precautionary principle could theoretically operate as a reversal of the burden of proof, shifting it from the entity opposing a potentially hazardous activity to the one wishing to carry it out. This means that those who want to engage in a potentially harmful activity must prove that it is safe, rather than those opposing it having to prove that it is harmful. This approach is logical in cases where there is a threat of serious and irreversible damage, as the necessary information about that threat is often in the hands of the party causing or threatening the damage. 

In the context of AI developers, it is argued that the burden of proof should similarly be transferred to them. They are expected to fully understand the threats posed by their products before placing them on the market. The document emphasizes that since the risks associated with AI systems can only be effectively addressed at the design stage, AI products should not be authorized for market placement until their potential adverse effects are fully understood, including any existential threats they may pose.
